image_description:
## 1) Chart type
- **Faceted timeline / career timeline chart** with **stacked interval blocks** for each person.

## 2) Layout techniques
- Uses **small multiples / faceting by candidate**: four vertical panels, one per candidate.
- Within each panel, career periods are shown as **stacked contiguous rectangles** along a shared vertical time/age scale.
- Uses **color coding** to distinguish career-category types.
- Panels are also grouped under **party headers** (Republican ticket, Democratic ticket).

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Candidate | Categorical/nominal | Faceting into separate vertical panels; name label at top |
| Party ticket | Categorical/nominal | Group header labels spanning panels |
| Age | Quantitative | Position on vertical axis (y-axis) with tick labels |
| Career moment / role | Categorical/nominal | Text labels inside blocks |
| Start year / event year | Temporal | Implied by vertical placement of block start and year labels in text |
| Duration / time span of role | Quantitative/temporal | Height/length of rectangular blocks |
| Career category (College, Military, Private sector, Public service or politics, Federal government, Candidate for federal office) | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue of blocks |
| Birth year / birthplace | Temporal + categorical/nominal | Subtitle text beneath candidate name |

comments.raw_comment: This graph is a very unique application of simple data collecting. In addition to providing us all with information concerning the travel efficiency, the commuter has also created a hobby which can occupy her time taking said train. Fortunately, many times the train is not excessively late as there are many gray areas in the scarf. In addition, these usually come in larger blocks of color symbolizing a longer span of days where the train was not too late. The pink areas are interspersed less often than the grey, but they occur regularly enough that one can assume that this train runs behind schedule for about a third of the time it runs. The red spaces, representing the longest wait time for trains or delays in both directions occurs much less often except in one outlier. On the right side of this graph, there is one solid chunk of red. This could represent a time when the transit system was dealing with renovations, working on a light schedule, or dealing with inclement weather, such as a season's worth of snow. Either way, there was a major obstacle in the Munich transit system which caused the train to be excessively late during that period. A good headline would be, "Weaving in and out of traffic".

comments.raw_comment: In this graph, I do not see something that looks like a graph at all. In all honesty I see a scarf. It is broken up into three separate colors: red, white, and blue. It could just be the weaver's preference of fabric, but I believe that it could relate to the different sides of the political spectrum. Rarely are the red and blue pictured next to each other, almost always separated by a stripe of white, a barrier of sorts. This could represent how most times, democrats and republicans are unable to work together to form policy in America. However, I do not know what the purpose of the width of the stripes means in this case. It probably represents some form of data, but I am unsure of whether it relates to laws being passed, or percentages of people getting laws passed.

This could have made them wake up earlier to take the train before the time they do so they can be on time for their jobs or activities.

comments.raw_comment: When examining this graph, the frontmost thought in my mind is that this is a very unique graph; I have never seen data represented by a scarf. Concurrently, I find it to be innovative and refreshing. Second to that, I notice that the thickness of the lines is greatest in the first two thirds of the scarf and thinnest towards the last one third. Based on this observation, I can infer that the woman experienced more frequent delays in the first two thirds of her year than she did in the remainder.  The wide red row also catches my eye. Both because red is indicative of a delay that was of more than half an hour or delays in both directions and because of its magnitude, I infer that there must have been an enormous accident that caused hours of delays, or perhaps even that the woman herself got into an accident. Since, as stated earlier, red represents up to 30 minute delays or delays in both directions and yet there lies this massive red row but also very slim red rows, I think the graph would be more logical if the woman incorporated a new color that would represent half an hour or greater. I wonder how this might compare to her commute in future years, as transportation technology continues to advance? Also, how would this graph differ if she decided to bike, walk, or take the train instead of driving to work?

comments.raw_comment: I noticed a few things about this graph. Firstly, there is a period in it where there was a delay of over 30 minutes for around a month in a row. Additionally, there are very many periods of 5 days in a row with grey. These are most likely periods of work days, Monday through Friday, where there are a lot of people commuting to work, increasing the number of time delays. I also noticed that there are periods of multiple days in a row with pink following the gray areas, meaning that there isn't very much traffic on the weekends in this area. I firstly wonder what could have inspired this scarf to be? Why did the creator decide to make this scarf based on their commute to work times? There are a lot of questions that can be asked about why this scarf was created and how inspiration was found to create it. I believe that in this graph a person is commuting to Munich for whatever reason, and that during their trips they are encountering a bit of traffic on the work days because there are also other people that are attempting to get to Munich to work. The period where there was an extended period of 30+ minute delays was most likely a main road closure. There is probably one main road that goes into Munich, and a side road or two. Since the main road was closed down, there was more traffic forced into the side roads, causing greater traffic backup and more time to get through the increase in traffic.

comments.raw_comment:
Welcome to Wednesday's moderation of  “What’s Going On in This Graph?”  
Today’s graph shows the length of daily delays for 2018 on what should be a 40-minute commute between Munich and a Bavarian town.  The commuter knitted two rows each day.  Grey is for delays under 5 minutes.  Pink is for delays 5 – 30 minutes.  Red is for delays over 30 minutes or delays in both directions.

From 9 am – 2 pm E.T. today, give us your responses online to these three questions -- "What do you notice?",  "What do you wonder?", and  "What's going on in this graph?"  
Plus, please have your students share with us a catchy headline that captures your ideas about the graph. 
Tomorrow afternoon, we’ll reveal the New York Times article that included this graph and much more.  We look forward to reading your discoveries.
(The next “What’s Going On in This Graph?” will be released tomorrow, Thursday, Feb. 28 with moderation on Wednesday, March 6.  The topic:  vaping.)
